Serving World Models on AWS Trainium with Native PyTorch

re:Invent · Code talk

Title · stays up during the introduction

Abstract. The next major leap in AI is predicting and interacting with the physical world. World models bridge digital reasoning with real-world execution, introducing new infrastructure demands for video generation, robotics, and gaming workloads. We’ll explore the emerging architecture of world models and why AWS Trainium, purpose-built for better price-performance, is well suited to serve them. Learn how native PyTorch support with torch.compile fuses operations into optimized device graphs, and how NKI custom kernels accelerate critical operators like attention. You’ll leave able to move world model inference from eager prototyping to compiled deployment using familiar PyTorch workflows.

Timing. The workload ~8 min · the hardware ~5 · idea 1 correct first ~5 · idea 2 big, reusable graphs ~10 · idea 3 precise control with NKI kernels ~13 · idea 4 split across cores ~6 · the result ~4 · cloud deployment ~7, only if there is time.

Intro · about 1 minute

The structure of the talk: four ideas for Trainium performance. Each one gets its own section and is shown on one worked example: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, a text + image to video model, one 704×544, 81-frame video with 10 denoising steps on one Trainium2 device (8 NeuronCores). Together they take it from 76.6 s in eager mode to 8.7 s per video. At the end we apply the same four ideas to a real world model, LingBot-World v2.

Each idea uses PyTorch the way you already know it: eager mode, torch.compile, torch.distributed, and NKI kernels called like torch ops. Every example ends with a takeaway you can apply to your own model.

Numbers are from RESULTS.md; code links are pinned to commit 788674b.

The pipeline we optimize, end to end

Section 1 · about 2 minutes · 4 clicks

The pipeline we optimize, end to end. Click 1, T5: encodes the prompt once per request.

Click 2, the DiT (diffusion transformer): denoises the latent video. In the outline’s words: 14B, 40 blocks, 7 chunks of 3 latent frames, 4,320 tokens per chunk, attending a KV cache of up to 17,280 keys; each chunk takes N = 4 denoise steps with no CFG, plus one forward that writes the chunk into the KV cache (skipped for the last chunk). That is 34 forwards, 1,360 block calls per video.

Click 3, the VAE: encodes the image, and decodes 21 latent frames into 81 frames of video. Click 4 clears the highlights.

CHECK: The outline’s DiT numbers (14B, 40 blocks, chunks, KV cache, no CFG) are LingBot-World v2’s; the worked example is Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (30 blocks, 10 steps with CFG). Say which model you mean, or use the 5B’s.

A world model: the same pipeline, extended three ways

World-trained
Realistic dynamics, steered by actions
Autoregressive
Chunk after chunk, with a KV cache
Streaming
Each chunk decoded as soon as it is ready

Section 1 · about 2 minutes · 3 clicks

1. Checkpoints trained to model the world: realistic dynamics, and conditioning on actions (move, turn, interact), not only on text.

2. Autoregressive: the same T5 → DiT → VAE, run chunk after chunk. The DiT keeps the KV cache from earlier chunks, so the scene stays consistent as the video goes on.

3. Streaming: the DiT hands each chunk of a few latent frames to the VAE as soon as it is ready. Pixels come out chunk by chunk while the DiT works on the next chunk. Sink and rolling caches bound the memory.

Talking point: “For the next 40 minutes we optimize the video diffusion pipeline: T5, DiT, VAE. Everything carries over to a world model. At the end we come back to a real one.”

A world model, chunk by chunk

Section 1 · about 1 minute · the animation plays when the slide opens (R restarts it)

Text feeds T5. Before each chunk the latest action (forward, up, down, forward, hold) lights up and goes into the DiT. The DiT makes the chunk, reading a KV cache that keeps a sink chunk and rolls the oldest out; each cache slot keeps the colour of the action it was made with.

Before the fourth chunk a new prompt goes through T5 again, while the KV cache is kept. Each chunk streams to the VAE and becomes frames whose camera follows the action, while the DiT works on the next chunk.

What this means for serving

Long sequences

Attention dominates compute.

→ Idea 3: precise control with NKI kernels

Many repeated calls

Per-call overhead matters.

→ Ideas 2 and 3: big graphs, less data movement

Two different halves

A matmul-heavy DiT, a convolution-heavy VAE.

→ Idea 2: compile where it pays

Latency per chunk

Time to the next frames is what counts.

→ The result: key press to new frames

Section 1 · about 2 minutes · 4 clicks

1. Attention over thousands of tokens dominates compute. 2. The same block graph runs hundreds of times, so per-call overhead matters. 3. The DiT is a regular, matmul-heavy transformer; the VAE is a chain of convolutions whose shapes change from chunk to chunk. 4. In a world model the user waits for each chunk, so time to the next frames is what counts.

Each implication points at the idea that answers it: long sequences → precise control with NKI kernels (idea 3); repeated calls → big, reusable graphs and fewer calls (ideas 2 and 3); two different halves → compile where it pays (idea 2); latency per chunk → the number the user actually feels, key press to new frames (S9d).

One node: 16 chips in a 2-D torus

16 × 8 chips × cores = 128
one node

→ Idea 4: split the work across cores

over NeuronLink · one each way in its row and in its column, wrapping at the edges

Why it mattersNo two cores are equally close, so the sharding plan is designed to fit this picture — that is idea 4.

Source: Trainium3

Section 2 · about 1 minute · 1 click

One node is 16 chips, 8 NeuronCores each: 128 cores. Each chip is wired to four neighbours over NeuronLink — the chips either side of it in its row of four, and the chips above and below it in its column — and both axes wrap, so there are no edges. That is a 4 × 4 2-D torus, and it is why the numbering matters: chip 0’s neighbours are 1, 3, 4 and 12.

The reason this slide is in the talk: the picture is not uniform. The 8 cores inside a chip are closer to each other — a faster interconnect, and the same HBM — than two chips are over NeuronLink, and a chip is closer to its four neighbours than to the chip diagonally opposite. So how you cut the work up is a decision about this shape, which is what idea 4 is about. No need to name any parallelism scheme here; the point is only that the distances differ.

If asked about core counts: a node can be configured to present two logical cores per physical core, and then neuron-ls reports 64 rather than 128. The numbers here are the physical cores. Not worth raising unprompted.

CHECK: the wiring and the numbering are read off neuron-ls’s CONNECTED DEVICES on a trn2.48xlarge — device d lists d±1 within its row of four and d±4 in its column, wrapping both ways. Our Trainium3 bring-up records the same node shape (16 chips × 8 cores = 128 physical cores, 144 GB HBM per chip). Confirm the Trainium3 table itself on the trn3 box before re:Invent. The footer now cites only the AWS Trainium3 page, so check that the page really does document the 4 × 4 wiring — if it does not, that citation is carrying a fact it cannot support, and the honest footer is “measured on the node”.

CHECK: “a faster interconnect inside a chip” is stated without a number on purpose. What we measured is one case — stage 2’s input gather over the 8 ranks of a chip against the same gather over 64 ranks across chips, where staying on the chip won by more than an order of magnitude — but that is one payload at one size and is dominated by the rendezvous, not a per-link figure. If anyone wants a number, quote NeuronLink-v4 from the AWS docs (S2b has it), not ours.

Idea

2

Give the compiler big, reusable graphs

Fewer, bigger graphs mean fewer launches and more fusion, and one compiled graph can serve every call of a repeated block.

With torch.compile(backend="neuron")

Section 4 · ~10 minutes

Idea 2. On Trainium the unit of work is a compiled graph, a NEFF. Bigger graphs mean fewer launches and more fusion, and one graph can serve every call of a repeated block. What you put inside one graph matters as much as compiling at all.

Idea 2 · Give the compiler big, reusable graphs

First attempt: fuse computation as one graph

Fuse the computationmodels/tp_utils.py
block.ffn = torch.compile(block.ffn, backend="neuron", dynamic=False)

To control what is not fused, you set the boundary yourself: @torch.compiler.disable keeps everything it wraps outside the graph — here, every collective.

Where the fusing stops
@torch.compiler.disabledef all_reduce_sum(x): ...

Section 4 · about 1 minute

The prototype compiled small modules — here the FFN — and marked the all-reduce as something the compiler must not absorb. @torch.compiler.disable is the knob for that: it forces a graph break, so everything it wraps stays outside. Worth knowing in its own right, and it is why one block reaches the device as several pieces rather than one.

The gaps are not Python, and the figure used to say they were. The host runs ahead of the device — a compiled graph and a collective are both enqueued asynchronously — so what sits between two pieces on the device is launch overhead in the Neuron runtime, not the interpreter executing. It matters because it says what the fix is: fewer, bigger pieces, not faster host code.

If asked why you would split it this way: it leaves one unknown instead of two. Compiling changes how the compute runs; tracing a collective changes how the ranks talk to each other. With the collectives left as the eager calls that already worked, anything that breaks is the compiler.

CHECK: the figure draws four graphs and three all-reduces for one block. Confirm that is the prototype’s real count before quoting it.

Idea 2 · Give the compiler big, reusable graphs

One graph per transformer block

One graph per blockmodels/fast_dit.py
import torch.distributed._functional_collectives as funcol​def _all_reduce(x):    return funcol.all_reduce(x, "sum", get_tp_group())   # traced: lives inside the graph​class _FastBlock(nn.Module):    def forward(self, x, e, cos, sin, ck, cv):        ...   # norm, QKV, RoPE, attention, FFN, all-reduces: the whole block​kw = dict(backend="neuron", dynamic=False, fullgraph=True)self.blocks = [torch.compile(_FastBlock(b, ...), **kw) for b in model.blocks]

Section 4 · about 2 minutes · live code

The collective becomes a functional collective, which the compiler traces, so it lives inside the graph. The whole block (norm + modulation, QKV, QK-norm, RoPE, attention, O-proj + all-reduce, cross-attention, FFN + all-reduce, gated residuals) is one module compiled with fullgraph=True.

If asked: the FFN (feed-forward network) runs every token through two large matmuls with an activation between them (here 3072 → 14336 → 3072), after the attention layers.

TakeawayCompile one graph per repeated block, with the collectives inside it.

Section 4 · about 2 minutes · 2 clicks

What the compiler does with that: 1. A larger optimization space. With the whole block in one graph the compiler picks the schedule — it fuses neighbouring ops so an intermediate can stay in SBUF, reorders work, and overlaps the HBM traffic that is left with computation. Say it that way rather than “no round trips per op”: the round trips do not vanish, there are fewer of them and the rest hide behind compute. 2. One launch per block instead of many. 3. Collectives scheduled by the compiler, next to the matmul that produces them. 4. One NEFF shared by all 30 DiT blocks: the weights are graph inputs, so one compile serves all 600 block calls — 30 blocks × 10 steps × 2 CFG passes.

CHECK: 30 is Wan2.2-TI2V-5B’s block count, and it is what makes the 600 calls add up. LingBot-World v2 is the 40-block model — the same mix-up S1a’s CHECK warns about.

Click 1, the result: also batch the two CFG passes into one call. DiT 4.4 → 1.91 s/step. Total 76.6 s → 36.8 s.

Click 2, the takeaway: Compile one graph per repeated block, with the collectives inside it.

Idea 2 · Give the compiler big, reusable graphs

Eager vs. one compiled graph

TakeawayFusion keeps data on chip: one read from HBM, one write back.

Section 4 · about 1 minute · the animation plays when the slide opens (R restarts it) · 1 click

Eager: six operations (norm, scale, shift, matmul, SiLU, add) run one after another. Each one is launched, reads its input from HBM, computes on one engine, and writes its result back to HBM, so the timeline fills with launch and memory time.

Fused with torch.compile: the same six operations are one graph with one launch. The data is read from HBM once, passes from operation to operation in on-chip SBUF while the engines overlap, and is written back once.

Demo idea: the same block, eager vs compiled, in the Neuron Explorer system trace. Many short executions with gaps become one long execution.

Click 1, the takeaway: Fusion keeps data on chip: one read from HBM, one write back.

TakeawayCompile where shapes are static and the compiler is strong; elsewhere, call a kernel.

Section 4 · about 2 minutes · 2 clicks

Compile is not always the answer. At 368×480×21: torch.compile across the whole VAE made 400+ graphs and ran out of memory; compiling the decoder took 58 minutes and ran in 11.5–12.9 s; a static-shape decoder in 2 graphs compiled in 20.6 minutes and ran in 12.8–14.2 s. Eager with NKI kernels: 1.7 s, no compile.

Why: the causal cache changes shapes from chunk to chunk, and the compiler’s 3D convolutions were slow. That sets up the next section.

Click 1: use small compiled graphs where they help: the VAE’s RMS_norm + SiLU is one tiny compiled function inside the eager model.

Click 2, the takeaway: Compile where shapes are static and the compiler is strong; elsewhere, call a kernel.

Idea 2 · Give the compiler big, reusable graphs

One VAE block, both ways

Section 4 · about 1 minute · the animation plays when the slide opens (R restarts it)

One Wan VAE decoder ResidualBlock: cache concat, RMS_norm, SiLU, conv3d 3×3×3, twice, then the shortcut add.

Eager with the NKI conv3d kernel: a launch gap before every op, short small ops, and convolutions at about 75% of peak, 1.7 s in total. Compiled with torch.compile: one graph per block, so the launch gaps and small ops nearly vanish, but the compiler’s own conv3d runs at roughly 12% of peak, so the same convolution work takes 11.5 to 12.9 s.

Idea 2 · Give the compiler big, reusable graphs

Why compiling does not always give the best performance

TakeawayThe compiler chooses a schedule by heuristic, under a search budget — so its choice is not always the best one.

Section 4 · about 2 minutes · 1 click

The point of the slide: a bigger graph is a bigger decision, not a guaranteed win — which is what the VAE on the last two slides was showing.

torch.compile turns your Python into a graph, in HLO, and that fixes what is computed: the operations and the values. It does not say how. The compiler decides that: how each tensor is laid out, how the work is cut into tiles, what order the instructions issue in, and which tensors hold on-chip memory — SBUF and PSUM — at each moment — and every one of those choices interacts with the others.

The number of combinations is enormous, and a compile has to finish in minutes, so the compiler does not search them — it uses heuristics. Usually they are good. On the VAE's 3-D convolutions they were not: the compiler's own version ran at roughly 12% of peak where the NKI kernel reached about 75%, which is the whole 11.5 s against 1.7 s.

Hand off to idea 3 here: when the heuristic picks badly for the one operator that dominates your model, you can make those choices yourself. That is what a kernel is.

CHECK: the figure draws four decisions with four options each, which is illustrative, not a real count. And confirm the wording for the graph the compiler consumes — HLO, as drawn, or StableHLO — since a Neuron audience will notice.

Idea

3

Precise control with NKI kernels

The compiler’s heuristics are general, and general is not always optimal. A kernel lets you decide how the computation and the data movement are scheduled on the hardware.

With Neuron Explorer, the profiler, and nkilib’s kernels

Section 5 · ~13 minutes

Idea 3. The compiler does well across a whole graph, but its heuristics are general. Where one operator dominates and the compiler’s version is not good enough, an NKI kernel gives you direct control over how the computation and the data movement are scheduled on the hardware — and you still call it from PyTorch, in eager mode or inside a compiled graph. What follows is one guideline with worked examples — keep the four engines busy. A second, move less data, is in backups B6a–B6d. Neither is a complete list.

Keep the four engines busy (this section, through S5j): each NeuronCore has four engines that can run at the same time, and speed comes from keeping them all busy. The profiler shows where they take turns; a kernel can overlap them.

Move less data is the guideline this section no longer shows: copies, kernel calls and small DMAs can cost more than the math, and in the world model most of the attention win came from moving less data rather than new math. Worth saying in a sentence if it fits; the examples are backups B6a–B6d.

Idea 3 · NKI · Keep the engines busy

What is still slow? Profile before writing a kernel

One compiled DiT block, native SDPA, one core: 56.1 ms

1

Three long Tensor gaps: ~22 of 56 ms

2

Vector + Scalar busy in the gaps: the softmax

3

Three times, once per head

Section 5 · about 3 minutes

The stage: one DiT block compiled as one graph (fullgraph=True) with native SDPA attention and no NKI. One core, one production rank’s shard: 3 heads × 2 CFG passes × 7,854 tokens. The pipeline at this stage takes 21.9 s (1.90 s/step). The block takes 56.1 ms.

1. The Tensor row has three long gaps: about 7–15 ms, 18–25 ms and 28–35 ms. That’s about 22 ms of a 56 ms block, nearly 40%, with the matmul engine doing nothing. (Tensor is also idle in short gaps elsewhere: the next slides’ 39% is its total busy time.) 2. During those gaps, Vector shows long dark-green bars and Scalar stays busy. That is the softmax of native SDPA: Vector computes the row max and row sum, Scalar the exp. In the utilization view (not on the slide) “Estimated Inst” drops to zero in exactly those windows.

Each Tensor burst after a gap is P×V; it waits for the whole softmax, and the Pending DMA spikes just before each burst (bottom of the screenshot) are the softmax output loading back from memory. 3. The pattern repeats three times, once for each of the 3 attention heads on this core. From about 35 ms on, Tensor is dense: output projection, cross-attention and FFN. That part is fine.

Profile: 1_compiled_no_nki/pairs/rank01_dit_56.14ms_c9eb70b86909 (.neff + .ntff), source 1_compiled_no_nki/source.tar.gz. Job wan2-ti2v-5b-tp8-nonki-job.yaml, script scripts/prof/block_pair.py.

Idea 3 · NKI · Keep the engines busy

Simplified: Tensor waits for the softmax

In the trace, max, exp and sum run tile by tile, so Vector and Scalar overlap. Either way, Tensor waits.

Section 5 · about 1 minute · the animation plays when the slide opens (R restarts it)

The same thing, simplified: one DiT block with native SDPA. For each of 3 attention heads the Tensor engine computes Q×K, then sits idle while Vector computes the row max, Scalar computes exp and Vector computes the row sum, then Tensor multiplies by V. After the three heads, Tensor runs cross-attention and the FFN densely.

The Tensor idle windows match the trace (about 7–15, 18–25 and 28–35 ms). The animation draws max, exp and sum as one step each; in the trace they run tile by tile, which is why the previous slide shows Vector and Scalar red through each whole gap.

Idea 3 · NKI · Keep the engines busy

Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI)

NKI
Write Trainium kernels in Python

You choose the tiling, the SBUF use, and which engine runs what.

nkilib
Common kernels, already optimized

attention_cte, conv3d, … written and tuned by kernel experts. Start here.

wrap_nki
A regular torch call

The same kernel in eager mode and inside a torch.compile graph.

Section 5 · about 1 minute

NKI is an interface, not a language: you write a Trainium kernel in Python, and you decide the things S4g showed the compiler deciding — the tiling, what sits in on-chip memory (SBUF), and which engine runs which part.

You usually do not start from scratch. nkilib ships the common kernels already written and tuned by people who do this full time — attention_cte, conv3d and more — and this talk uses them directly. Reach for nkilib first; write your own when nothing fits.

And it stays ordinary PyTorch: wrap_nki turns a kernel into a regular torch call, so the same kernel runs in eager mode and inside a torch.compile graph with no separate code path.

Idea 3 · NKI · Keep the engines busy

Attention: the operator that dominates

Section 5 · about 1 minute · 1 click

At 7,854 tokens, self-attention through the default SDPA path took 18.2 ms per call. Click 1: nkilib attention_cte, exact flash attention, 5.3 ms per call. This kernel is the attention win in this talk.

If asked about softmax shortcuts: a constant-max kernel on top of attention_cte is a much smaller step. On Wan2.2 it saves ~0.3 s per video (7.2 → 6.9 s on a later build, checked version in de63a5d); on LingBot-World v2 it is backup B6d, with its check.

Section 5 · about 2 minutes

The same block, same shard, same core, with nkilib attention_cte for self- and cross-attention. The pipeline in this configuration takes 9.7 s on the Kubernetes job (8.7 s in RESULTS.md from a Docker run).

What the timeline shows (block = 17.3 ms): 1. Self-attention runs from about 3.3 to 8.0 ms (the long red bar on TensorMatrix): about 5 ms for all three heads, against about 32 ms with native SDPA. 2. The Tensor row has no gaps in that window, and Vector and Scalar are busy in the same window: the softmax runs at the same time as the matmuls instead of between them. 3. The selected instruction is the kernel’s Q×K nc_matmul of a Q tile with one K tile, inside its K-tile loop (in the code view); the next step, masking + scale + max reduce, runs on Vector while Tensor moves on to the next K tile. The short red bar at about 10.3–11.1 ms is cross-attention, also attention_cte, under 1 ms. Everything else is the QKV, output projection and FFN matmuls, dense on Tensor.

The pale-green box is the selected instruction’s details; it covers the Tensor row from about 8 to 17 ms. The TensorMatrix row under it is clear.

Split the work across cores

The frame rate needs more than one chip. Which axis crosses a chip boundary is a choice about the topology — and then you measure it.

With torch.distributed and functional collectives

Section 6 · ~6 minutes

Idea 4. The parallelism is plain torch.distributed and functional collectives, traced into the compiled graphs. The section answers three questions in order: why one chip is not enough (S7a), which axis goes where and why (S7b), and what that looks like in code (S7d). Backup B7c measures four layouts against each other inside a single device.

Idea 4 · Split the work across cores

The frame rate decides how many chips

TakeawayA watchable frame rate needs more chips than one, so the only question left is how the work is split.

Section 6 · about 1 minute · 1 click

Why this section exists at all. A world model is watched while it runs, so the frame rate is the requirement, not a score. At 25 fps a frame has to be finished every 40 ms, and that is not something one chip does for this model: 8 chips reach 18.64 fps, 16 reach 25.02.

Both figures are without the softmax check, so they compare like with like — the guarded 8-chip number is 18.40 (S9c, and its CHECK).

So the question is not whether to split the work but along which axis, and that is what the next slide answers from the topology.

Idea 4 · Split the work across cores

Put the chatty collective where the links are fast

TakeawayShard so the frequent collective stays inside a chip, and only the cheap one crosses between them.

Section 6 · about 2 minutes · 1 click

This is the justification for the layout, and it comes from S2c. Cores inside a chip exchange data faster than chips do over NeuronLink. So the plan is not a preference, it follows from that: put the group that talks most inside a chip, and let the axis with the cheaper collective be the one that crosses.

Tensor parallel goes inside a chip. Every block all-reduces twice — after the attention output projection and after the FFN — on every forward. Keeping that group within one chip means those all-reduces never touch NeuronLink.

Sequence parallel goes across chips. Each chip holds a slice of the tokens, and what has to cross is the key/value all-gather: once per block, and only the K and V of this chunk rather than every activation.

Then measure it, because the reasoning gives you a candidate and not a result: S7d is what it looks like in code, and backup B7c measures four layouts against each other inside one device.

CHECK: the plan is deliberately stated without numbers. These runs are TP4 × CP16 on 16 devices and TP4 × CP8 on half a trn3 (S7d's notes), where 4 is a chip's logical cores as that node is configured; the lnc=1 configuration puts 8 physical cores in the group. Decide which one the talk presents before a number goes on this slide.

The journey on one Trainium2 device: 76.6 s eager; 36.8 s with torch.compile, one graph per block; 16.1 s with the VAE tiled over 8 cores and the NKI conv kernels; 10.8 s with NKI attention, CFG-parallel and sequence parallel; 8.7 s with VAE fusion and the host fixes.

LingBot-World v2: 25 fps on 16 devices, 18.4 on 8

Section 7 · about 1 minute · 1 click

LingBot-World v2, 81 frames at 480×768, 4 denoise steps. On 16 trn2 devices, from the upstream port at 11.90 s (6.81 fps) to 3.24 s (25.02 fps): 3.68× end to end. Four runs of the final flags gave 24.99–25.04 fps, so 25 fps is reached with no margin. GEN is the DiT and T5; VAE is the decoder.

Rows in full: upstream port, TP8 × CP8 (8.95 + 2.95 s); + merged attention, SP, FiLM all-to-all (5.75 + 3.01 s); + VAE fused and bf16, paired KV chunks (4.48 + 0.81 s, q6); + host fixes, VAE -O1 and 2-D tiles (4.04 + 0.33 s, q14); + vendored kernel: grouped V loads, rank-blocked K (3.66 + 0.31 s, q20); + attention calls chained in the kernel, V token-major, the runtime I/O descriptor cache (q21–q24, 3.60 s, 22.49 fps), then the constant offset in 34 layers (B6d; q25, 3.06 + 0.30 s); + less work before the first block: KV caches kept across generations, host setup in background threads, the camera MLP on each rank’s own tokens (q30–q33, 2.93 + 0.31 s).

Cloud deployment · on Amazon EKS

From the device to the cluster

Section 8 · about 1 minute · the animation plays when the slide opens (R restarts it)

It opens the section because it travels outwards: the device becomes half a pod, the other half holds the code and the weights, and then four identical pods sit under one EKS cluster. Everything before this section was inside the box; everything from here is around it.

The device becomes the left half of a pod whose right half holds the model code and the weights. kube-scheduler asks the Neuron DRA driver for NeuronCores, the driver allocates the device, and the scheduler places the pod. Finally an EKS cluster frames everything: four identical pods, served by one scheduler and one DRA driver.

Section 8 · about 2 minutes · 5 clicks

serve_ti2v.py serves the same compiled pipeline the benchmark measures. It runs FastAPI on rank 0 (POST /generate, /health, /readiness), with all 8 ranks in one torchrun.

1. Fixed shape: every request image is resized and cropped to the warm-up size, so no request triggers a compile. 2. Collectives stay on one thread: they must run on the thread that compiled the graphs, so HTTP requests go on a queue and the main thread runs them. 3. T5 on the CPU, with a prompt cache: it is needed for every request, and it does not fit in HBM next to the DiT and VAE. 4. Health before readiness: /health answers while the model loads; /readiness turns true only after warm-up.

Click 5, the takeaway: Fix the input shapes, so no request ever triggers a compile.

NOT FOR THE TALK: the links drawn between the cores are a schematic ring, not this chip’s topology, and the device is Trainium2 while the work is now Trainium3. S2b covers the same ground — 8 cores, SBUF, the four engines, the collectives — from the AWS docs. Kept only as a record.

One Trainium2 device exposes 8 NeuronCores in LNC1 mode. Each core has four engines that run at the same time: Tensor for matmuls, Vector for elementwise work and reductions, Scalar for activations such as exp, and GpSimd for general-purpose work, plus on-chip SBUF memory. The cores are linked for fast in-device collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter); tensor and sequence parallelism ride on these links.

The outline also says: the whole pipeline (5B DiT, T5 and VAE) fits on one device’s HBM.

Backup: LingBot VAE, step by step

Backup · the tuning steps behind B4i

Step by step on 64 ranks: whole blocks compiled with the halos in the graphs (1.36 s, within 1.8e-5 of the per-conv decoder); bf16 convolutions with norms, softmax and the output conv in fp32 (0.80 s); compiler -O1 and the norm sums as a matmul (0.55 s); 2-D height × width tiles instead of width slices (0.33 s); 6 latent frames per step (0.31 s).

Norm as a matmul: the channel sum of squares as one fp32 matmul against a ones vector. The default form cost ~174 ms of Tensor time and 64 ms of GpSimd cross-lane reduce (vae2_1_fused.py).

The 2-D tiles also fixed a quality bug: width slices padded the 96-wide latent to 128 by repeating its last column, which leaked into real pixels (43.5 dB). Tiles need no padding.

Did not help: skipping the halos entirely (a diagnostic) was slower, 0.95 s, so halos were not the cost; 1 / 4 / 10 / 20 frames per step gave 1.35 / 1.19 / 1.21 / 1.93 s.

CHECK: The dB column reads 56.6 from the bf16 step on, but the padding bug behind the 43.5 dB was fixed by the 2-D tiles, two rows later. Confirm what each dB is measured against.

Use it if someone asks whether compiling ever wins on a VAE.

Same lesson, opposite result. LingBot’s upstream decoder ran each latent frame as dozens of tiny graphs and eager ops, with the halo exchange between ranks issued from the host: about 3 s, of which only 0.2 s is convolution.

Click 1: one compiled graph per decoder block, with the halo exchange inside it as functional collectives. Click 2: the VAE drops to 1.36 s, and to 0.31 s after more tuning. The decision is the scope of the graph, not compile vs. no compile.

If asked: upstream it is ~33 single-conv graphs, ~200 eager ops and 33 host-issued halo all-gathers per latent frame (2.95 s in the upstream job, 3.01 s on our branch before this change; 1.36 s is measured against the 3.01). The tuning steps after 1.36 s are on backup slide B4h.

for kc, vc in zip(k_chunks, v_chunks):          # the cache's own chunks, read in place    o, neg_max, s = _attention_cte(q_c, kc, vc, ..., skip_output_normalization=True)# out = sum_c exp(m_c - M) O_c / sum_c exp(m_c - M) S_c

Backup · move less data, cut from idea 3 · 1 click

Cut from the talk, with B6b–B6d: this is the second guideline, move less data, and its example is attention over a cached KV window — chunked flash attention with the softmax merged across the chunks. Two things make it a bad fit for the time available: it is hard to say why this had to be built rather than called, and the merge itself means explaining online softmax to a room where not everyone has met flash attention. The guideline still holds — copies, kernel calls and small DMAs can cost more than the math, so read data where it is, in the layout it arrives in — and these four slides are the evidence if anyone asks.

Now the world model. Its DiT attends a list of cached chunks: a sink plus a rolling window, up to 17,280 keys. The kernel was fine; what surrounded it was not.

Before every call, the upstream code copied all the chunks into one padded buffer. That copy took 1.7 ms of a 10.4 ms block. It was also wrong: the padding keys entered every softmax, which scaled the outputs by 0.94–0.99.

Click 1, the fix: one kernel call per chunk, reading each chunk where it already is, then merge the results. The next slide shows why the merge is exact.

If asked: no bounds were passed to the kernel, so the zero keys counted (flat heads scaled by 0.993, by 0.939 in the first chunk). At CP16 the copy also cost 3.1 s per forward for the second chunk. The flag is LINGBOT_CTE_MERGE=1.

Backup · move less data, cut from idea 3 · the animation plays when the slide opens (R restarts it) · 2 clicks

One query against three cached chunks of four keys. The bars are the query’s attention weights.

Step 1, one kernel call per chunk: each call reads its chunk in place. Inside a call, the softmax is taken against that chunk’s own maximum, so every chunk’s tallest bar reaches the same line. The kernel returns the result without normalizing it, plus the chunk’s max and sum.

Step 2, rescale to the global max: the merge multiplies each chunk by how far its max is below the largest one: ×1, ×0.37, ×0.17.

Step 3, the check: the dashed outlines are one softmax over all twelve keys, as if the chunks had been copied into one buffer. They match exactly: the merge is exact, not an approximation.

Results: GEN (the DiT and T5) 8.95 → 5.73 s, together with sequence parallelism. Click 1: then fewer, fuller calls: two chunks per call, 3.28 → 2.88 ms per block.

If asked: the factor is exp(mc − M), applied to each chunk’s output and sum: out = Σ exp(mc − M)·Oc / Σ exp(mc − M)·Sc, in fp32 on small per-row stats. Gain 1.0000 on every head. 5.73 s is the job’s TP8 × CP8 layout; TP4 × CP16 (the layout in S9c) gives 5.75 s. Two chunks per call: each call costs ~0.15 ms whatever its size, and the first chunk goes in as the kernel’s prefix-cache prior, the same softmax over their union (model_fast.py, LINGBOT_ATTN_PAIR=1; GEN 4.88 → 4.48 s).

Click 2, the takeaway: Don’t copy data to fit a kernel: call it where the data is, and merge the results.

A recap of the world model’s attention work. None of these changed the math. 1. No copies: read the cache where it is (the last two slides). 2. Fewer calls: every call has a fixed cost, so give each call more work. 3. Fewer DMAs: load data in bigger pieces, and read it in the layout it arrives in instead of permuting it first.

Backup: a softmax shortcut that checks itself

Subtract one constant instead of the running max: exact, but only while the scores stay in range

~2× faster
per attention call

of a video: the cost of the check

TakeawayA numerical shortcut must check its own result, and fall back to the exact path.

Backup · the softmax shortcut, cut from idea 3 · 3 clicks

Back to idea 1, inside a kernel: one numerical shortcut, made safe. A softmax normally tracks a running maximum, to keep exp() in range. LingBot-World v2 skips that in 34 of its 40 layers: it subtracts one fixed constant instead. Subtracting the same number from every score doesn’t change the softmax, so the result is exact, but only while the scores stay in a range. We measured that range on one clip. Nothing guarantees it for another input, and outside it the output is NaN.

So the kernel checks its own result. Click 1: every row is checked, and any block with a row out of range is redone exactly, inside the same kernel. Nothing goes back to the host, which matters in a stream: the frames are already on their way.

Click 2, the result: attention calls are about 2× faster; the output stays exact even when we force the scores out of range, where the unchecked kernel gives NaN; and the check costs about 1% of a video.

Talking point: random inputs don’t find a shortcut’s limits, and one clip doesn’t either. If you take a numerical shortcut, make the kernel check its own result and fall back to the exact path.

If asked: the constant is 30; a row is in range when its sum Σ exp(s − 30) lies between e−60 and e78. One core, four chunks: 0.70 → 0.35–0.37 ms per call. Forced out of range = layer 10’s queries scaled ×32: every block is redone and lands 3.4e-3 from exact attention. On the clip, 0 of 1.85 M blocks are redone. Cost: +39–52 ms of generation on 8 devices (18.64 → 18.40 fps). A layer that redoes more than 5% of its blocks moves to exact attention. Why one constant works, and the code: backups B6g and B6h. Source: kiro/LOOP_ENGINEERING.md at ad34d57.

Click 3, the takeaway: A numerical shortcut must check its own result, and fall back to the exact path.

CHECK: The 2× per call is the shortcut without the check (16 devices, one core); the ~1% cost is measured on 8 devices, where the check is validated end to end. At CP16 (16 devices) the check is validated on one core only, and the 25 fps runs are without it.

  2. 2

Backup · detail behind B6c

nkilib attention_cte copied into the repo (kernels/attention_cte_lb.py), every change marked lingbot: behind its own flag, and checked bitwise against nkilib at every DiT call shape (kiro/attn_bitcmp.py).

1. V tiles 8 per DMA (LINGBOT_CTE_VGROUP=8): each software-DGE dma_copy costs ~0.75 µs of GpSimd time whatever its size, and there were ~800 per call. GEN 3.94 → 3.74 s. 2. K read in the layout the CP all-gather leaves it (LINGBOT_K_BLOCKED=1): no permute, plus a dead cache write skipped. GEN 3.74 → 3.66 s. 3. Cross-attention cache stored in the kernel’s layout: two strided transposes gone, ~250 µs of a 3.2 ms block.

Did not work: runtime-built DMA descriptors (faster per block, but rebuilt whenever the 40 blocks bind different buffers: GEN 4.26 vs 3.94 s); K+V double buffering (does not fit SBUF); one call over all 17,280 keys (0.72 vs 0.68 ms).

Backup · detail behind B6c · 1 click

Where the time is now, one block (2.53–2.60 ms, TP4 × CP16): ~350 µs of all engines idle waiting for the K/V all-gathers, ~100 µs of K/V loads at the start of each call, ~150 µs merging (almost all data layout), FFN ~310 µs.

Click 1, talking point: “Most of the attention win was not new math. It was fewer kernel calls, fewer DMAs per call, and no copies around the kernel. The profiler showed which one each time.”

Correctness: only DMAs changed, yet some ranks move by up to 6.2e-3 (output RMS 0.515): one fp32 ulp in the row sum. An autoregressive rollout amplifies any rounding change, so the gate is chunk 0 against fp32 (0.0125, upstream 0.0257), determinism, and the video.

Backup: why one constant works in 34 of 40 layers

softmax(QKᵀ − c)·V with one constant c = 30, in 34 of 40 layers

0.70 → ~0.36 ms
per call (one core, four chunks)
3.30 → 3.06 s
GEN per video, 16 devices: a late, modest step

Backup · detail behind B6d · 3 clicks

The online softmax spends part of every kernel call on the running row max, the rescaling of the accumulator and a transpose of the probabilities. A constant offset c skips all three: the kernel computes softmax(QKᵀ − c)·V with an fp32 [V | 1] accumulator. Subtracting the same c from a row doesn’t change its softmax, so it is exact as long as nothing overflows or underflows: for c = 30, while every row max m satisfies −85 < m − 30 < 78, i.e. m between −55 and 108.

Click 1: a diagnostic run (LINGBOT_ROWMAX_GRAPH=1) recorded the row maxes over a whole generation on all 64 ranks: 34 layers stay within [−8.3, 71.5], a margin of at least 36 on both sides. Click 2: layers 2, 13, 33, 34, 38 and 39 reach 126–864 in one or two heads; they keep the exact chained attention_cte calls.

Click 3: one core, four chunks: 0.35–0.37 ms per call instead of 0.70 ms; the block at lead 3: 1.97 instead of 2.31 ms. End to end on 16 devices (q24 → q25): GEN 3.30 → 3.06 s, 22.49 → 24.12 fps, a ~7% GEN step late in the journey, not a main driver. Block output vs the exact chained calls: rel. RMS ≤ 1.4e-3 on all 64 ranks.

The catch: the range was measured on one clip. Nothing guarantees it for another input. B6d shows the check.

Sources: kernels/attention_cmax2_lb.py, kiro/LOOP_ENGINEERING.md (“The constant-offset attention (q25)”).

CHECK: A version with one offset per layer diverged after chunk 3 and was dropped; don’t claim per-layer offsets.

Backup · detail behind B6d

The guard’s runtime branch. _guard_check flags every block slot with a row out of band and exchanges the flags between the two physical cores. nl.fori_loop over a count loaded into a register is a runtime branch: one taken if any block failed, one per block inside it. Argument lists shortened with “...”.

Four layouts on the same 8 cores, one per click: tensor parallel over 8 cores with CFG as a batch of 2 (29.4 ms per block, 13.2 s total); CFG-parallel, two groups of 4, one per CFG pass (24.5 ms, 11.9 s); plus sequence parallelism, all-gather / reduce-scatter around the matmuls (21.9 ms, 11.1 s); plus cross-attention local to each core’s tokens (20.6 ms, 10.8 s).

What is only here is the “what is new” card: a KV cache that lives across calls, and a DiT → VAE handoff per chunk. Worth showing if someone asks what a world model adds to a video model.

LingBot-World v2 (technology.robbyant.com) is built on Wan2.2. It is the same T5 → DiT → VAE, but causal (autoregressive), conditioned on actions, with an unbounded horizon, and a distilled fast variant for real time.

Click 1, what carries over: block-compiled DiT graphs, NKI attention, collectives in the graph, and a VAE that decodes chunk by chunk with nkilib convs. Click 2, what is new: a KV cache that lives across calls, and a DiT → VAE handoff per chunk.

The point of the callback: nothing in the four ideas was specific to video diffusion. The world model needed the same ideas; only the data flow is new.

Backup: four ideas for Trainium performance

1
Correct first

Check every step, and every shortcut, against a correct eager run.

Example: within the bf16 floor, and 44.6 dB on the VAE

2
Give the compiler big, reusable graphs

One graph per repeated block, with the collectives inside it.

Example: 76.6 → 36.8 s per video

3
Precise control with NKI kernels

Overlap the four engines, and move less data: no copies, fewer calls, bigger DMAs.

Example: block 56.1 → 17.3 ms; LingBot attention reads its cache in place

4
Split the work across cores

Give each core its own share, with the collectives inside the graph.

Example: 29.4 → 20.6 ms per DiT block

Backup · the closing recap, if you want one

Cut from the talk: the four ideas are named on S0a at the start and each one carries its own takeaway line, so a closing recap was the most cuttable two minutes in the deck. Put it back if the talk runs short, or show it while taking questions.

The four ideas, each with the example that showed it. These are the takeaways.

1. Correct first. Start in eager mode on the neuron device; it gives a correct baseline with minimal changes. Check every later step against it, and if a kernel takes a numerical shortcut, have it check its own result at run time and fall back to the exact path — backup B6d is one.

2. Big, reusable graphs. Compile with torch.compile(backend="neuron") and choose the scope: one graph per repeated block, with the collectives inside it. Where shapes change or the compiler is weak, call a kernel instead.

3. Precise control with NKI kernels. Profile first, find where the four engines take turns, and use a kernel that overlaps them — and remember that copies, calls and small DMAs often cost more than the math. Reach for nkilib before writing your own.

4. Split across cores. Plain torch.distributed and functional collectives, traced into the graph; measure the layout.

If asked about serving: fixed shapes so no request triggers a compile, warm up until the timing settles before reporting ready, and host work off the device’s path — the cloud-deployment section, S11b to S11d.

Backup: from the engines to the cluster, uncut

Backup · the uncut version, about 30 s · the animation plays when the slide opens (R restarts it)

This is the full-length original. S11a plays the same animation from the moment the device becomes a pod; this one starts two beats earlier, inside the chip: the four engines of one core lighting in turn, then an all-gather around the ring of eight cores until every core holds every block. Worth showing if someone asks what a collective actually does, or wants the whole zoom-out in one picture.

A Trainium2 device with 8 NeuronCores. Inside one core the Tensor, Vector, Scalar and GpSimd engines light up in turn next to on-chip memory. Then collectives move data between the cores: an all-gather around a ring, until every core holds every block.

Then the device becomes the left half of a pod whose right half holds the model code and the weights. kube-scheduler asks the Neuron DRA driver for NeuronCores, the driver allocates the device, and the scheduler places the pod. Finally an EKS cluster frames everything: four identical pods, served by one scheduler and one DRA driver.
